title: Evaluate Division
notes:
Task and constraints: Answer ratio queries from equations a/b=value, returning -1.0 when variables are unknown or disconnected; each query searches a weighted graph.
Idea: Each equation adds directed edges with weight v and reciprocal 1/v. dfs returns 1 when source equals target, marks visited nodes, and multiplies edge weights by recursive results until a route is found; queries with unknown variables return -1.0.
Technique and why it applies: Weighted graph traversal composes ratios along a path, since a/c equals (a/b)*(b/c).
Invariant: The accumulated product along the active DFS path represents source divided by the current variable; visited prevents cycling through the same variable.
Edge cases: Unknown variables return -1.0; a known variable queried against itself returns 1.0; disconnected known variables exhaust DFS and return -1.0. The code assumes consistent nonzero equation values.
Complexity: Building the graph is O(V+E), and each query can visit O(V+E), giving O(Q(V+E)) time and O(V+E) graph storage.
complexity_reason: Each equation adds two graph edges and each query may traverse all vertices and edges; graph adjacency and per-query visited sets use O(V+E) space.

title: Evaluate Division
notes:
Task and constraints: Evaluate ratio queries from equations and return -1.0 if no connecting path exists; edge weights represent directed ratios and reciprocals.
Idea: The method builds adjacency lists of Object[] pairs containing neighbor and weight. Each known query calls dfs with product 1.0; dfs returns product at the target, otherwise multiplies it by each edge weight during recursion and returns the first successful result.
Technique and why it applies: Weighted DFS composes ratios along a path and a visited set prevents revisiting variables in cycles.
Invariant: product equals the ratio from the query's source to the current node along the active path; a successful recursive return carries the complete source-to-target ratio.
Edge cases: Unknown variables yield -1.0; a known variable divided by itself yields 1.0; disconnected nodes return -1.0. Values must be nonzero for reciprocal edges, and floating-point products may accumulate rounding error.
Complexity: Graph construction is O(V+E), and Q DFS calls cost O(Q(V+E)) worst case; graph and visited state use O(V+E) space.
complexity_reason: The adjacency graph stores two directed edges per equation, and each DFS query may examine every edge and vertex.

title: Nth Digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the digit at one-based position n in the concatenation 1234567891011...; the method skips entire groups of numbers with equal digit length.
Idea: length, count, and start describe the current digit-width block. While n exceeds that block's digit count, it subtracts the block size and scales all three values. It then computes the containing number and digit offset, converts the number to a string, and returns that character as an integer.
Technique and why it applies: Digit-block arithmetic skips groups in bulk instead of generating every preceding number.
Invariant: After each loop iteration, n is the one-based position within the remaining block of numbers having digit length length, whose first number is start.
Edge cases: n=1 returns 1; positions at a block boundary move to the next digit length; zero-based digit indexing is obtained using (n-1)%length. n is assumed positive.
Complexity: The digit length grows logarithmically with n, giving O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The loop advances through digit lengths logarithmically, then converts only the target number to a string.

title: Nth Digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the digit at one-based sequence position n in 1234567891011... by counting digit-length blocks.
Idea: pos, len, count, and start use long arithmetic. Whole blocks are subtracted until pos fits; the target number is start+(pos-1)/len and its character index is (pos-1)%len. The digit is returned by subtracting '0' from the selected character.
Technique and why it applies: Counting numbers and digits by width avoids iterating through every number before the requested position.
Invariant: pos remains the one-based offset within the active len-digit block, and start is the first number in that block.
Edge cases: n=1 returns 1; a position exactly after a block boundary enters the next block; long intermediates prevent overflow in len*count and number calculations under expected constraints. charAt index is within the number string.
Complexity: There are O(log n) block iterations and a constant-size final conversion, with O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The loop processes one iteration per digit length and uses long scalars plus the target number's short string.

title: Binary Watch
notes:
Task and constraints: List all valid binary-watch times with exactly turnedOn LEDs lit; hours range from 0 to 11 and minutes from 0 to 59.
Idea: Nested loops enumerate every hour-minute pair. The sum of h.bit_count() and m.bit_count() is compared with turnedOn, and matching times are formatted as hour plus a two-digit minute.
Technique and why it applies: Exhaustive enumeration is practical because the clock has a fixed 720 possible times, so no search pruning is necessary.
Invariant: After each pair is checked, out contains exactly the valid times among pairs already visited.
Edge cases: turnedOn=0 returns only "0:00"; impossible counts return an empty list; minute 5 formats as "05". The method relies on the fixed clock ranges rather than scaling with an input-sized domain.
Complexity: It checks 12×60 pairs, which is O(1) for this fixed domain; output space is proportional to the number of matching times.
time_complexity: O(1) for the fixed clock domain
complexity_reason: The method examines a fixed 720 hour-minute pairs and stores only matching formatted times.

title: Binary Watch
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all hour-minute pairs whose binary representations contain exactly turnedOn set bits; hours and minutes are limited to the fixed watch ranges.
Idea: The nested loops cover hours 0..11 and minutes 0..59. Integer.bitCount totals the set bits, and String.format writes each matching time with a two-digit minute.
Technique and why it applies: Direct enumeration is sufficient for the constant-size clock domain and guarantees every possible valid time is considered.
Invariant: out contains precisely the qualifying times among the pairs already checked, without duplicates because each pair is visited once.
Edge cases: turnedOn=0 includes "0:00"; values too large for any hour-minute bit count produce an empty list; String.format("%d:%02d",...) preserves a leading zero for single-digit minutes.
Complexity: The loops inspect 720 pairs, constant work per pair; space is O(1) for the fixed domain plus the returned list.
time_complexity: O(1) for the fixed clock domain
complexity_reason: The loops check exactly 720 combinations and retain only matching strings in out.

title: Remove K Digits
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove exactly k digits from a decimal string to minimize the resulting nonnegative number; the result is returned without leading zeroes.
Idea: Each digit is processed in order. While removals remain and the stack's last digit is larger than the current digit, that larger digit is popped. The digit is then pushed; any remaining k digits are removed from the end, and leading zeroes are stripped.
Technique and why it applies: A monotonic increasing stack greedily removes an earlier larger digit when a smaller later digit can move left to reduce the number's value.
Invariant: After processing a prefix, stack is the smallest retained prefix for the number of removals already used, with digits in nondecreasing order where the greedy condition allowed it.
Edge cases: k equal to string length returns "0" after stripping; increasing digits may leave removals to trim from the end; all-zero results normalize to "0". Input is assumed to have valid k.
Complexity: Each digit is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) stack space.
complexity_reason: Each digit is pushed once and popped at most once; the stack and final output can each contain O(n) digits.

title: Remove K Digits
notes:
Task and constraints: Delete k digits from a nonnegative decimal string to obtain the smallest number, then remove leading zeroes and return "0" if empty.
Idea: A char array acts as a stack with top as its size. For each digit, larger trailing digits are removed while k remains; the digit is appended. Remaining removals shrink top from the end, then leading zeroes are skipped before constructing the result.
Technique and why it applies: A monotonic stack makes a smaller digit replace a larger earlier digit whenever deletion budget remains, minimizing the most significant positions first.
Invariant: st[0..top) contains the retained prefix after processing digits so far, and top tracks the valid stack length.
Edge cases: k may remove every digit and yields "0"; increasing input uses leftover deletions at the end; leading zeroes are skipped after deletion. Math.max(0,top-k) prevents a negative length, and substring bounds stay within the char array.
Complexity: Every digit is inserted once and removed at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The char-array stack receives each input digit once and removes at most n digits, with O(n) storage.

title: Frog Jump
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a frog can reach the final sorted stone, starting with a jump of one and changing each jump length by at most one.
Idea: Lists shorter than two return true; if the second stone is not at position one, it returns false. Each stone maps to a set of jump lengths reaching it. For every known jump k, the code tries k-1, k, and k+1 and records positive jumps landing on an existing stone.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic reachability stores possible last jump lengths per stone, because future moves depend on both position and the previous jump.
Invariant: jumps[x] contains exactly the jump lengths discovered that can land on stone x; processing each one propagates all legal next lengths.
Edge cases: A single stone returns true; a second stone not at 1 fails immediately; jump lengths of zero or less are ignored. The set-based state prevents duplicate propagation of identical jumps.
Complexity: Up to O(n) jump lengths can occur at each of n stones, giving O(n²) worst-case time and space.
complexity_reason: The per-stone sets may hold O(n) jump lengths each, and each stored jump tries three transitions.

title: Frog Jump
notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether the frog can reach the last stone when each jump differs from the previous by at most one; reachable states include both stone position and jump size.
Idea: The method rejects a second stone not at 1. It maps every stone to a set of jump lengths, seeds position zero with jump zero, and propagates k-1 through k+1 when positive and landing on an existing stone. A copied set avoids modifying the set during iteration.
Technique and why it applies: Reachability DP stores distinct jump lengths at each position, allowing future moves to depend on the previous jump without repeating equivalent states.
Invariant: Each set contains discovered jump sizes that can land on its stone, and every processed size generates all legal next sizes.
Edge cases: Fewer than two stones returns true; a missing first jump of one returns false; nonpositive candidate jumps are ignored. new ArrayList<>(...) avoids concurrent modification while destination sets are updated.
Complexity: There are O(n²) possible position/jump states and three transitions per state, giving O(n²) time and space.
complexity_reason: The map holds a set of reachable jump sizes per stone, and each state checks three possible next jump lengths.

title: Sum of Left Leaves
notes:
Task and constraints: Sum values of left leaf nodes in a binary tree; a node counts only if it is a leaf and is the left child of its parent.
Idea: Null roots return zero. If root.left exists, the code adds its value directly when it has no children; otherwise it recurses into that left subtree. It always recurses into the right subtree, where left leaves may occur deeper.
Technique and why it applies: Recursive DFS examines subtrees while the parent-child relationship identifies whether a leaf is specifically a left child.
Invariant: Each call returns the sum of left leaves within its subtree, excluding right leaves and non-leaf left children themselves.
Edge cases: An empty tree returns zero; a root that is itself a leaf contributes nothing because it has no parent marking it as left; a left child with children is traversed instead of counted directly.
Complexity: Each node is visited at most once for O(n) time, and recursive frames use O(h) space.
complexity_reason: The recursion visits each node at most once and uses stack frames proportional to tree height h.

title: Sum of Left Leaves
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the sum of values for nodes that are leaves and are left children; a right leaf is never included merely because it is a leaf.
Idea: Null returns zero. When root.left exists, the method adds its value if both child references are null, otherwise recursively sums left leaves beneath it. It also recursively processes root.right.
Technique and why it applies: DFS combines subtree sums, while checking the left child at its parent distinguishes left leaves from right leaves.
Invariant: The returned sum includes every left leaf in the current subtree exactly once and excludes the current root unless it is counted by its parent.
Edge cases: Null trees return zero; a lone root returns zero; a left leaf contributes its value, while a right leaf is excluded. Recursion depth can reach the tree height.
Complexity: Each node is inspected once, so time is O(n); recursion uses O(h) stack space.
complexity_reason: Each tree node is visited at most once, and recursive calls retain O(h) frames.

title: Convert a Number to Hexadecimal
notes:
Task and constraints: Convert a signed 32-bit integer to lowercase hexadecimal without a built-in converter; negative values must be represented using their 32-bit two's-complement form.
Idea: Zero returns "0". Other values are masked with 0xffffffff, then each low nibble selects a character from digits and the number shifts right four bits until zero. Reversing the collected digits gives the final hexadecimal string.
Technique and why it applies: Nibble extraction reads four bits at a time, and the mask limits negative Python integers to the intended unsigned 32-bit representation.
Invariant: At each loop, out contains the low-order hexadecimal digits already extracted in reverse order, and num contains the unprocessed higher bits.
Edge cases: Zero takes the special return; 26 becomes "1a"; -1 becomes "ffffffff" after masking. The 32-bit mask is essential because Python integers are arbitrary precision and negative right shifts are sign-extending.
Complexity: At most eight nibbles are processed for a fixed 32-bit input, so time and space are O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop extracts at most eight hexadecimal nibbles and stores them in a short list.

title: Convert a Number to Hexadecimal
notes:
Task and constraints: Return lowercase hexadecimal for a signed 32-bit integer without conversion helpers; negative values use their 32-bit two's-complement representation.
Idea: Zero returns immediately. Otherwise each iteration appends digits[num&15] and performs an unsigned right shift by four, then reverses the StringBuilder.
Technique and why it applies: Four-bit nibble extraction maps directly to one hexadecimal digit; unsigned shift ensures negative int values eventually reach zero after eight nibbles.
Invariant: The builder contains extracted low-order digits in reverse order, while num holds the remaining high-order bits.
Edge cases: Zero returns "0"; 26 becomes "1a"; -1 produces eight f digits. The >>> operator is important because >> would keep filling high bits with ones for negative values. StringBuilder avoids repeated immutable concatenation.
Complexity: A 32-bit int needs at most eight iterations, so time and auxiliary space are O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop performs at most eight nibble extractions and stores them in a bounded StringBuilder.

title: Queue Reconstruction by Height
notes:
Task and constraints: Reconstruct a queue from [height,k] pairs, where k counts people ahead with height at least the person's height; the returned order must satisfy every pair.
Idea: people is sorted by height descending and k ascending for ties. Each person is inserted at index k in out, placing exactly k already-processed people before them who are at least as tall.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy insertion works tallest-first because shorter people inserted later cannot affect the count of people at least as tall for those already placed.
Invariant: After each insertion, all processed people satisfy their required count of preceding people with height at least their own.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list; tallest people with k=0 are inserted at the front; equal-height people are ordered by k so their constraints remain consistent. Python list insertion shifts elements and is not constant time.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n) and n list insertions cost O(n²) overall; output uses O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Sorting is O(n log n), but inserting each person into a Python list may shift O(n) elements, giving O(n²) time and O(n) storage.

title: Queue Reconstruction by Height
notes:
Task and constraints: Rebuild the queue so each [height,k] person has exactly k preceding people whose height is at least theirs.
Idea: Arrays.sort orders heights descending and k ascending for equal heights. Each pair is inserted into an ArrayList at index k, and toArray converts the final list to int[][] output.
Technique and why it applies: Processing tallest people first makes each insertion's position equal the required count of already placed people at least as tall; shorter later people do not alter that count.
Invariant: Every inserted person has the correct number of preceding people with height at least theirs, and future insertions preserve this property.
Edge cases: Empty input yields an empty two-dimensional array; k=0 inserts at the front; equal heights are processed in ascending k order. ArrayList insertion shifts later elements, so it is linear per insertion.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n), list insertions dominate at O(n²), and the list plus returned array use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The list may shift O(n) entries for each of n insertions; sorting and output conversion are lower-order compared with O(n²) insertion.

title: Trapping Rain Water II
notes:
Task and constraints: Compute trapped water in a height map; boundary cells cannot hold water, and the lowest current boundary determines how far water can be contained inward.
Idea: Small maps return zero. All boundary cells enter a min-heap and are marked seen. The heap pops the lowest effective boundary; each unseen neighbor is marked, water adds max(0,h-nh), and the neighbor is pushed at effective height max(h,nh).
Technique and why it applies: Boundary-driven priority flood expands from the lowest escape boundary, so each interior cell's water level is determined by the minimum enclosing boundary height reached.
Invariant: Every heap entry represents a discovered cell with its effective escape height, and seen prevents processing a cell twice.
Edge cases: Fewer than three rows or columns trap no water; a basin cell below its boundary adds the height difference; high interior cells add zero. Rectangular nonempty input is assumed.
Complexity: Each of mn cells is pushed and popped once with heap operations, giving O(mn log(mn)) time and O(mn) space.
complexity_reason: Every cell enters the heap at most once and heap operations cost O(log(mn)); seen and the heap hold O(mn) cells.

title: Trapping Rain Water II
notes:
Task and constraints: Calculate water trapped in a 2D height map by expanding inward from the boundary; the smallest effective boundary height controls each newly reached cell.
Idea: Small grids return zero. add inserts each unique boundary cell into a min-priority queue. Each poll explores four neighbors, marks unseen cells, adds max(0,curHeight-groundHeight), and pushes them with effective height max(curHeight,groundHeight).
Technique and why it applies: A min-heap priority flood always expands the lowest available boundary first, ensuring the effective height passed inward reflects the lowest escape level.
Invariant: Each queued cell has an effective water boundary height; once seen, a cell is queued only once and its contribution is computed when reached.
Edge cases: Grids under three rows or columns return zero; an interior depression adds positive water; a neighbor taller than the current boundary contributes no water and raises the propagated height. The code assumes a nonempty rectangular matrix.
Complexity: Each cell is inserted and removed once with logarithmic heap work, giving O(mn log(mn)) time and O(mn) space.
complexity_reason: The priority queue and seen matrix store up to mn cells, and each cell incurs one logarithmic heap insertion and removal.

title: Longest Palindrome
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum palindrome length constructible from the characters of s; character order may change, and at most one odd-frequency character can occupy the center.
Idea: Counter obtains each character count. For every count n, the method adds its largest even contribution (n//2)*2 and records whether any count is odd; it adds one center position if so.
Technique and why it applies: Parity counting pairs equal characters on opposite sides of the palindrome and reserves one leftover character for the center.
Invariant: length contains all usable paired characters from counts processed so far, while odd records whether a center character is available.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; a single character yields one; several odd counts contribute pairs from each but only one extra center position. Python Counter supports arbitrary characters.
Complexity: Counting and iterating over u distinct characters takes O(n) time and O(u) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The string is counted once and the distinct-character counts are processed once; Counter stores O(u) entries.

title: Longest Palindrome
notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the maximum palindrome length from a string's characters, pairing equal characters and allowing one odd leftover in the center.
Idea: A 128-entry count array is filled from s. Each count contributes its largest even value n/2*2 to len, and odd tracks whether any character has an odd count; the result adds one if odd is true.
Technique and why it applies: Character parity determines how many copies can form symmetric pairs; at most one unpaired character can be used as the center.
Invariant: len is the sum of pairable copies across processed character codes, and odd records whether a center candidate exists.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; a one-character ASCII string returns one; multiple odd counts add only one center. The fixed array assumes characters fit indices 0..127, so arbitrary Unicode chars outside ASCII can cause an array-index error.
Complexity: Filling counts and scanning the 128 entries take O(n) time; the fixed frequency array uses O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The input string is scanned once and the fixed 128-entry frequency array is scanned once, using constant auxiliary storage.
